title: Implement the project check pipeline from discovery to verdict
acceptance: One orchestrator runs the stages of docs/architecture/CHECK_PIPELINE.md in order, calling the modules the earlier phases built rather than reimplementing any of them.

sure check PATH performs a real check - findings, checked/not-checked scope and an overall verdict - instead of exiting 3, and sure recheck and sure repair reach the same orchestrator through Command::report rather than a second path into the engine.
A stage that did not run, whether skipped, refused by the execution mode, unconfigured or errored, is recorded as such, and no stage in that state can aggregate to a clean verdict.
A dynamic check runs only where the selected execution mode authorises it; where it does not, the result is not checked and never passed.

The exit status follows docs/architecture/CLI.md - 0 for a clean project, 1 for a project that was checked and is not clean, 5 for a run that tried and did not finish - and the run states what it did not check.

title: Calibrate finding severity and evidence class against the acceptance corpus
acceptance: Each release-blocking case in evaluation/acceptance-manifest.json whose fixture app exists under fixtures/adversarial/ yields a finding at the severity the manifest names, observed by running it and asserted by a test rather than by a report.

The rule that decides between note, can_fix_later and must_fix for a detector finding is written where the detectors and the aggregator can both be read against it, and false_completion_aggregator::is_style_noise follows that rule instead of deciding on its own.
The benign cases do not move: benign-test-mocks stays note, demo-analytics and lying-readme stay should_fix_first, and no finding about a test-only mock becomes must_fix.
Severity is not raised by relabelling: a finding the code cannot ground keeps its evidence class, and a detector that needs must_fix earns it by anchoring, not by declaring inference a fact.
evaluation/acceptance-manifest.json is unchanged - it is the requirement, not the implementation.

title: Make the ubuntu and macos jobs green again, and keep them read
acceptance: A run of the `ci` workflow on this branch has all five jobs green — `rust (windows-latest)`, `rust (ubuntu-latest)`, `rust (macos-latest)`, `shellcheck-secondary` and `bootstrap-validate-windows` — and the run id is named in the hand-back so the claim can be checked rather than believed.
On ubuntu and macos the test step actually executes: the log for each contains `test result:` lines and a passed count, rather than the job ending at clippy. The counts are reported per platform.

Every test that fails on a platform is either fixed or shown to be asserting that platform’s own path semantics, and in the second case it is gated to that platform with a comment saying why — the choice is made per test with the reason written down, not by disabling a suite.

The classification question is answered rather than assumed: `candidate_context::classify_path` and `recording_projection` decide by walking `path.components()`, so a Windows-style path given to them on Unix is one component and classifies differently from the same path on Windows, while `hook_protection`’s `folded` normalises `\` to `/` on every platform on purpose. Whether a path that arrives from outside the process must be normalised is stated in the code where it is decided, together with the effect the current answer has on a verdict.

Whatever is fixed is fixed in the source and not in the workflow: no job is made to skip a test, continue on error, or run a narrower command than it ran before, unless the hand-back says exactly which line changed and why that is not a way of not looking.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor, from a check of the branch's own CI runs, and placed first in the array so §14 dispatches it next. The `ci` workflow has failed on 75 consecutive runs. The last green run is 35193436468 (commit 6d69c51b, 2026-09-17T07:13Z); the first red is 35196110213 (commit 717fc0ad, 2026-09-17T07:45Z). The run table in progress/HANDOFF.md stops at 35174114907, which is before the last green run, so none of the streak is recorded anywhere and the loop has been treating five green Windows gates as the whole story. Three distinct causes were seen: (1) `cargo test` failing on `rust (windows-latest)` in 35196110213, where three tests in `crates/sure-core/tests/browser_driver.rs` (:367 `a_page_that_never_arrives_is_a_failure_of_the_project_and_not_an_absence`, :474 `a_healthy_local_page_is_opened_and_comes_back_green`, :550 `a_page_that_throws_and_asks_for_something_missing_reports_all_of_it`) panicked with `a browser was found at C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe and could not be driven: Absence { reason: DriverWouldNotStart, detail: "...ran for 19.999018 seconds without reporting a debugging port" }` — that message is the product's own false-green discipline working correctly, and the job is green today, so this cause is environmental or intermittent and must be characterised rather than assumed fixed; (2) `cargo test` failing on `rust (ubuntu-latest)`, with `candidate_context::tests::windows_separators_work` (panicking at crates/sure-core/src/candidate_context.rs:134) and `recording_projection::tests::file_write_event_is_projected` (panicking at crates/sure-core/src/recording_projection.rs:734) — both are the same root cause, and it is not merely a test problem: `classify_path` (candidate_context.rs:36-60) decides by iterating `path.components()`, so `tests\\foo.rs` is two components on Windows and one on Unix and classifies as Test there and Product here, and the projection's `basename` would be `src\\main.rs` on Unix rather than `main.rs`; `hook_protection.rs:1015`'s `folded` already takes the opposite position by normalising backslashes on every platform, because a harness may send either, so the codebase holds two incompatible answers and this task decides which is right and says so where it is decided; (3) `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` failing on ubuntu and macos, which is the current shape and starts with commit 752489c (`P12-T010`, pushed 2026-09-18T16:36Z) — three helpers in `crates/sure-testkit/tests/integration_thinness.rs` (`powershell` :438, `launcher_scratch` :453, `stub_binary` :474) are live only on Windows, so on Unix they are dead code and `-D warnings` fails the job, and because clippy runs before the tests the test step has NOT RUN on Unix since then, which is why cause (2)'s current status is unknown. Causes (2) and (3) are the class of defect a Windows-primary machine cannot see from its own gates, which is the whole reason CLAUDE.md requires CI portability. Do not 'fix' this by weakening a job: the point is to learn what the Unix jobs know, not to stop them saying it. The supervisor is handling the record-keeping half — the run table and the streak's absence from it — so this task does not need to write progress/. Relationship to the other CI tasks: this is not a duplicate of P15-T010 ("Create cross-platform CI matrix"), whose acceptance already requires the macOS and Linux core jobs to be mandatory, nor of P16-T003 ("Run final cross-platform core gates"), whose acceptance requires the required Windows/macOS/Linux jobs to be green for the final commit. It is the task that makes both satisfiable — the matrix exists and two of its three platforms have been failing unread — so P16-T003 cannot honestly be accepted until this one is done. P15-T011 ("Create GitHub release workflow/checksums") depends on P15-T010 and is unaffected by this task except that a release built while two platforms were red would have been built from a tree nobody had verified on them.

title: Make the non-Windows configuration checkable from Windows
acceptance: A single documented command runs on this Windows machine, needs no administrator rights and no WSL, and fails when the non-Windows `cfg` set would fail to compile or would trip lints — the class that produced 75 red CI runs without ever being reproducible locally.

The command is demonstrated against the real defect rather than asserted to work: a `#[cfg(windows)]`-only helper is reintroduced ungated, the command is run and shown to fail by naming it, and the helper is removed again. Both outputs are quoted in the hand-back.

Its cost is measured and stated as a wall-clock figure, because a check nobody can afford to run is a check nobody runs, and the figure decides whether it belongs in the local gate set listed in CLAUDE.md or in a slower pre-push path.

Whatever it needs installed is written down with the install command, and the check reports what is missing rather than failing obscurely when it is absent — a developer who cannot run it should be told to install a target, not left to decode a linker error.

If no such command can be made to work from native Windows, that is a valid outcome only with the attempts recorded and the reason spelled out: what was tried, what it did, and what a developer on Windows is then supposed to do instead. "It did not work" without the attempts is not an answer.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor, from the investigation of the 75-run CI failure streak recorded at item 99 of progress/HANDOFF.md. The streak's three significant defects — `candidate_context::tests::windows_separators_work` and `recording_projection::tests::file_write_event_is_projected` failing on Unix, `recheck_lifecycle::tests::keys_match_case_insensitively_on_windows` failing on its own Unix branch, and three helpers in `crates/sure-testkit/tests/integration_thinness.rs` that are live only on Windows and so are dead code under `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` — share one property: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` on Windows compiles the Windows cfg set, in which those helpers are used, so the failures are unreproducible on the only machine this loop develops on. The class is caught, by design, on ubuntu and macos — but only there, and only if someone reads the run. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` pins toolchain 1.98.1 and runs fmt, check, clippy, test on a three-OS matrix; nothing in the repository passes `--target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` or `--target x86_64-apple-darwin`, there is no pre-push hook, and there is no local substitute. So the blind spot is structural rather than a missed step, and the fix is a local command rather than more discipline. Candidates to evaluate rather than assume: `rustup target add` plus `cargo check --target <triple>` or `cargo clippy --target <triple>`, which needs no linker for check-only work; a `cfg`-auditing pass over the source; or building the Windows cfg set with the non-Windows arms forced, which is cheaper but less faithful. Constraint from CLAUDE.md: this must work natively on Windows and must not require moving anything into WSL, so a WSL-only answer does not satisfy the task. Note the asymmetry that made this class invisible for so long and that the acceptance is designed around: the same commit added four helpers, three ungated Windows-only and one used from an ungated test, and only the three produced errors. Measured on 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while verifying P15-T016, which narrows this task from "is it possible" to "how far does it reach". `rustup target list --installed` on this Windows machine already lists `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` and `x86_64-apple-darwin`, and `cargo clippy -p sure-testkit --all-targets --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -- -D warnings` exits 0 (in 0.15 s, cached; P15-T016's worker ran it uncached and used a deliberate `#[cfg(not(windows))]` dead-code probe to confirm the command really compiles that file for Linux rather than doing nothing). The same target does NOT reach the crates that link SQLite: `cargo check -p sure-core --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` exits 101 inside `cc-rs` with `error occurred in cc-rs: failed to find tool "x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc": program not found`, because the bundled `libsqlite3-sys` needs a cross C compiler this machine does not have. So acceptance criterion four has a measured answer for `sure-testkit` and an open one for `sure-core` and `sure-cli`: either a cross toolchain is installed and written down with its install command, or the check is scoped to the crates it can cover and names the ones it cannot — a crate that cannot be checked must not be silently treated as checked.

title: Tell a person when a recorded allowance cannot be spent
acceptance: Recording an allowance in a project whose settings make every matching request unanswerable by that allowance does not end in a plain success: the command either refuses and says why, or records and says what will actually happen — observed by running it in such a project and reading what it writes, not by reading the code.

The reason is stated in the user’s terms and names the setting that causes it, so a person can change that setting or stop expecting the allowance to work; it does not name the internal mode value alone.

The confirmation a user reads when an allowance *can* be spent no longer promises an outcome the settings make unreachable, and the confirmation for one that cannot is a different sentence rather than the same sentence plus a caveat.

Whatever is chosen, the store is left consistent with it: an allowance that is refused is not written, and one that is written is one a matching request can actually spend. Proved by reading the store back after both cases.
The command still records an allowance for every project where one can be spent, so the fix does not narrow what P13-T005 delivered.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor, from P13-T005's verification. Driven through target/debug/sure.exe against a scratch project outside the repository, with the payload the supervisor wrote: a project whose sure.yaml says `execution: mode: inspect_only`, then `hook allow-once --project <that project> --tool Shell --command "rm -rf build/"` exits 0 and prints "SURE recorded a one-time allowance for tool 'Shell', for the request 'rm -rf build/'." followed by "SURE would then let that one request through, if SURE names it as deleting a whole location, overwriting published commits, or reading a file of credentials." The request it was recorded for is then still blocked, unchanged, with "The current execution mode does not permit this action." — and it stays blocked however many times it is sent. The cause is not a bug in the spend path: under a mode that does not run project code, `consent::decide_for` answers an arbitrary command `Denied` rather than `NeedsConsent` (`crates/sure-core/src/consent.rs:491-501`, because `CommandClass::Destructive.required_permission()` is `None` at `crates/sure-domain/src/execution.rs:631`), and `hook_protection::assess_request` reads a danger only for `NeedsConsent` (`crates/sure-core/src/hook_protection.rs:426-429`), so no danger is ever named and `with_any_allowance` returns at its first line (`crates/sure-cli/src/hook.rs:416-418`). That refusal is deliberate and correct — `docs/security/PROTECTION_MODE.md` states that a request held for any other reason cannot be let through by an allowance, and "an allowance is not a way to run under settings the user did not change". What is wrong is only what the user is told at the moment they record the grant: the command has `--project`, could read the mode, and instead reports a success and a promise that this project's settings make unreachable. The safe direction holds throughout — nothing dangerous is allowed — so this is a false reassurance and a silent no-op, not a false green. Related but distinct: `docs/security/PROTECTION_MODE.md` says the *subject* is deliberately not checked at write time, because there is no request to read then, and a grant no request ever matches is spent by nothing and expires; that stays as it is and this task does not ask for it. The mode, unlike the subject, is knowable at write time.

notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor, from P13-T004's verification. crates/sure-cli/tests/cli_contract.rs's a_directory_of_our_own allocates from a fixed pool of 1,000 candidates — `{what}-{NEXT}`, NEXT per-process from 0, made unique by create_dir — and the helper's own doc comment says it is never cleared, for a good reason (clearing a fixed path and then treating it as fresh fails on Windows, where a deletion can fail silently, and the test then describes a directory that was never emptied). The two together are the defect: never clearing is right, a fixed 1,000-name budget is not, and when every candidate collides the helper panics with "no free directory under ...". Measured at P13-T004's acceptance: all 1,000 of store-0 .. store-999 existed — 1,340 directories, every one named store-N or project-N, no files — so the_protection_mode_a_project_names_is_the_one_sure_decides_under failed when run alone and would have failed in a full run. The accepted gate run at 1454c8e was green and consumed the last headroom; one full suite run allocates about 123 names, so it recurs after roughly eight runs. The supervisor cleared the scratch subtree and the gates re-ran green, which buys about eight runs and fixes nothing. This is the verification instrument, not the product: the failure is loud and on a correct tree, and the damage it does is to make a worker doubt its own change or edit product code around it. It belongs beside P15-T010 (cross-platform CI matrix) and P16-T003 (final cross-platform core gates), both of which need the suite to run repeatedly on one machine.

title: Ask the volume, not the operating system, whether two paths are one file
acceptance: The claim is measured before anything is changed: on the macOS CI job, or any macOS machine this loop can drive, two spellings of one path (`src/EMAIL/SEND.rs` and `src/email/send.rs`) are put to the filesystem and what it answers is quoted with the command that asked. If on that machine they are two different files, this task's premise is wrong and its valid outcome is to be closed with that measurement recorded and no code changed around it — "the premise held" is not to be assumed from the platform's name.

The mechanism is chosen rather than assumed. `recheck_lifecycle::normalise_path` (`crates/sure-core/src/recheck_lifecycle.rs:57-67`) folds case under `#[cfg(windows)]` and is the question's whole answer today; it is compiled into `FindingKey::new`, so it decides whether a previous finding matches this run's finding. Case sensitivity belongs to the volume and not to the operating system — macOS ships case-insensitive volumes by default and can also hold case-sensitive ones, and a Linux mount can be either — so whatever replaces this must say at the decision what it is asking, what it does when it cannot tell, and which way it errs when it cannot tell.

The consequence is stated as a verdict-level effect and not only as a test: two spellings of one file must not become two findings for one issue, and a previous finding must not be carried open beside this run's copy of it. The hand-back says which of those the current code does, on which platform, measured rather than reasoned.

A test pins the behaviour on every platform. Any assertion that has to differ by platform says what it is asking that platform and why, in the pattern P15-T016 landed in `candidate_context` and `recheck_lifecycle`; a loosened or removed assertion is not an answer.

Anything that cannot be run on the machine this loop develops on is reported as not measured rather than inferred, and a check that a filesystem probe needs in order to be meaningful states what it does when the probe itself fails.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor, from P15-T016's hand-back and the supervisor's own reading of the code. The reading: `normalise_path` (`recheck_lifecycle.rs:57-67`) returns `trimmed.to_lowercase()` under `#[cfg(windows)]` and `trimmed.to_owned()` otherwise; it is called from `FindingKey::new` for both `location` and `locator`, so the key that decides whether a previous finding is the same finding is case-folded on Windows and case-preserving everywhere else — including the macOS jobs, whose `#[cfg(not(windows))]` branch is the one P15-T016's worker had to correct. The consequence P15-T016 measured on a case-sensitive filesystem: `keys_match_case_insensitively_on_windows` reports two findings for what Windows reports as one, and the previous finding is carried open beside the current one rather than matched. That is correct on Linux and is the open question on macOS, where the default volume is case-insensitive, so the same two spellings name one file and SURE reports it twice. Nothing about this is a false green — it is duplicate material and a missed match, not a pass — which is why it is a task with its own acceptance rather than a stop-the-line like P15-T016. It is deliberately not answered inside P15-T016: the fix moves what the product reports on a supported platform, and that is a decision with evidence of its own. Related but distinct: P4-T007's case-sensitivity work is about the check plan and the fixtures it added are what the Unix branch of that test exercises; this task is about the reconciler's identity question.

title: Make the program a test executes one that nothing is still writing
acceptance: Every fixture that copies a file and then executes it is found and listed, not only the ones already named. The record that prompts this task names two fixtures; `grep -rn "fs::copy" crates/*/tests/` finds four call sites, and the hand-back lists each with the command that found it and says for each whether the thing it copies is later executed. A fixture that copies a binary and runs it and is left off that list is a fixture left unfixed.

The mechanism is stated as the kernel's rule and not as a story about threads. `ETXTBSY` is raised at `execve` when the inode being executed is open for writing by *any* process; `fork` duplicates the descriptor table into the child, which is how a write descriptor held by one thread's `fs::copy` comes to be held by another thread's about-to-`execve` child; and `O_CLOEXEC` closes that descriptor at the child's own `execve`, which is the moment just after the window that matters. The hand-back says which of these the fix rests on, which it does not, and which of them it could not check from this machine.

The path that is executed is never a path with an open write descriptor. Whatever form the fix takes, the inode at the executed path must be complete and closed before anything can execute it — the proposal already recorded is to copy to a unique temporary name, close, and rename into place — and the hand-back says what window is left afterwards and why it is narrower, argued from the mechanism in the previous criterion rather than from the failure having become rarer.

The residual window is treated as a property of `fork` rather than as something a fix removes, and any retry is bounded, named and placed deliberately. If a retry is added, the hand-back says which error it retries and which errors it passes through unchanged, what the bound is, and where it lives. A retry in `sure-core`'s product code that exists so that a test can pass is not an answer: the product's job where it stands is to report what the operating system said, and in every recorded occurrence it did exactly that — `Error`, never a pass. A retry inside a fixture must not be able to turn a program that genuinely cannot be started into a pass.

What was reproduced is separated from what was reasoned. Windows has no `ETXTBSY`, so the platform that fails is not a platform this loop can run, and anything demonstrated instead — a test of the rule the fix rests on, a reading of the fixture that shows the executed path is closed, or a run of the suite under load — is reported as what it is. A criterion that cannot be met on this machine is reported as not met rather than inferred from the platform's name.

The verification is a number of runs and not the word "fixed". The falsifier already in `progress/HANDOFF.md` says a flake that has stopped appearing has not thereby been explained. The hand-back names how many executions of the `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` step of `rust (ubuntu-latest)` came back with zero failures, with their run ids, and states what would falsify the change. Until that number exists, the honest closing sentence is the one the existing section already ends on.

The record is corrected where it is wrong rather than only added to. The existing section and the P5-T003 run rows name two fixtures and say the failure rate is unknown; the hand-back corrects them in place — the number of call sites, the occurrences as they then stand, and whether the rate is still unknown — in the pattern the sections around them are kept in. A section left saying two when the tree has more is a correction the next reader will not get.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while verifying P15-T016 and reading the ubuntu re-run of 35389096745. The evidence is already in this repository three times over and never had an owner. progress/HANDOFF.md's P5-T003 run row for 35086572733 records the first occurrence: `rust (ubuntu-latest)` failed `a_service_that_outlives_the_window_and_then_ends_is_still_a_failure` and `service_supervisor.rs::a_service_that_is_dropped_is_stopped_anyway` with `Text file busy (os error 26)`, and the re-run of that one job came back green. The row for 35087849335 records the second: the same errno, a third and fourth distinct test, on a commit that changes three files under progress/ that no compiler reads. The section under those rows derives the mechanism -- `fs::copy` holds the destination open O_WRONLY for the whole copy of a multi-megabyte binary, `fork` copies that descriptor into a child, and `execve` of that inode inside the window is refused -- names the fix (copy to a unique temporary name, close, rename into place, plus a bounded retry on ETXTBSY because the fork window is not removable), and states the falsifier: THE TASK THAT NEXT TOUCHES EITHER FIXTURE MAKES THE CHANGE AND RECORDS N RUNS CLEAN RATHER THAN THE WORD FIXED. No task touches either fixture and none had been minted for it, so that falsifier has been pointing at nobody since 2026-09-16. THE THIRD OCCURRENCE IS THE ONE THAT MINTED THIS TASK: on 853d7de -- the first commit on this branch whose tree lets the ubuntu test step run at all, which is what P15-T016 exists to restore -- the step ran and `a_service_that_outlives_the_window_and_then_ends_is_still_a_failure` failed at crates/sure-core/tests/runtime_start.rs:1450 with left Error against right Fail and the same errno inside SURE's own sentence, having already passed in the same binary on the run before. Only one test failed and --no-fail-fast carried the rest of the suite, so the run's ubuntu failure is exactly this. The log as it stood before the re-run replaced it is kept at target/tmp/ci-35389096745-ubuntu.log. THE CALL SITES ARE MORE THAN THE RECORD SAYS, which is the first thing this task has to fix: `grep -rn "fs::copy" crates/*/tests/` on 2026-09-19 finds four, and three of them execute what they copy -- Fixture::python at crates/sure-core/tests/runtime_start.rs:397, as_python at crates/sure-core/tests/service_supervisor.rs:180, and the copy that names a program with a space and a non-ASCII character at crates/sure-core/tests/process_runner.rs:691 -- while copy_tree at crates/sure-core/tests/rust_fixture_apps.rs:194 copies fixture sources and executes none of them. The record names two and the tree has three, which is the same shape of gap this file's own item 99 was about: a claim about the whole tree made from a sample of it. WHY THIS IS A TASK AND NOT A STOP-THE-LINE, since P15-T016 was placed first in the array for a reason and this one deliberately is not: nothing here is a false green. Every recorded occurrence is the product reporting `Error` rather than a pass, in the operating system's own words, and the failure names itself in the log with a path and an errno that nothing else in the suite produces, so a reader can tell it from a real failure without a re-run. The cost is a re-run of one job per affected run and the record-keeping that goes with the re-run replacing the failure in the run's own state, which is expensive and is not a correctness defect. It is also a cost this task's own verification cannot compress -- the fix is verified by n green ubuntu runs, and those arrive one push at a time whether the task is dispatched now or later -- so moving it ahead of P13-T006 would buy nothing except a delay to the feature work, which is not what §14's reordering exception is for. THE CONDITION THAT REOPENS THAT CALL: if a genuine ubuntu failure is ever mistaken for this one, or if this one fails a tree that cannot be its cause twice more, the ordering decision is to be reopened rather than defended, because at that point the flake is hiding failures rather than merely adding a re-run. Related but distinct and deliberately not merged: P15-T016 owns the CI jobs reaching their tests at all, and P15-T017 owns whether the non-Windows configuration can be checked from this machine; this task owns one race in this repository's own fixtures, which is why it is placed after both of them rather than beside them.

title: Give the checksum manifest a reader, or take it out of the tree
acceptance: The premise is measured and the measurement is in the hand-back, not asserted from this task's notes. Two things are shown with the command that showed them: that nothing in the repository reads `SHA256SUMS.txt` — no script, no workflow, no test, no Rust code, only prose about it — and that both of the bootstrap gates exit 0 over a manifest that is out of date. A hand-back that repeats this task's own sentence back is not a measurement.

The outcome is a decision that is stated as one. Keeping a file nothing reads is not neutral: it looks like assurance, and a reader who finds it will assume something checks it. The two honest outcomes are to give it a reader or to remove it and say what, if anything, took over its job. Either is acceptable and the hand-back argues for the one it chose; leaving it unread while saying nothing is not, because then its only function is to look like a check.

If it stays, what the check hashes is stated, and it is the same form the manifest was built from. `.gitattributes` sets `eol=crlf` for some paths, so the index blob and the checkout differ in length for those — measured on 2026-09-19: `scripts/install.ps1` is 2388 bytes in the index and 2426 bytes in the working tree, and a check that compares a working-tree digest against an index-derived manifest reports two mismatches that are not staleness. The hand-back says which of the two the check reads and why, and the answer is checked by running it against a manifest known to be correct.

If it gets a reader, that reader runs where a reader can fail. It joins the local gate set and a CI job, or the hand-back gives a written reason why not — and "the check would be red" is not a reason, because a check that is red because the manifest is stale is telling the truth about the tree. A check that runs only when someone remembers to run it is the situation this task exists to end, one level up.

The means of maintaining the file is in the repository, or the file is gone. `target/tmp/regen-sums.mjs` is currently the only thing that can regenerate it and `target/` is not committed, so no contributor has it — measured: `find . -name "regen-sums*" -not -path "./target/*"` returns nothing. Whatever the decision, the hand-back says where the regeneration lives after it, and a contributor on a fresh clone can follow that sentence to a file that exists.

The check does not make the commit rhythm impossible, and the hand-back says what a contributor must run before committing. The manifest hashes `progress/HANDOFF.md`, `progress/state.json` and `tasks/tasks.json`, so every acceptance commit changes three files it covers — measured: `grep -cE "^[0-9a-f]{64}  (progress|tasks)/" SHA256SUMS.txt` is 8, four under each. A check that is guaranteed red on the commit that records an acceptance is worse than no check, and the flow that satisfies it — stage, regenerate, commit — is either the one this loop already follows or the one the task replaces it with, stated plainly enough to be followed on the next task.

The self-reference is answered rather than left to be discovered. `SHA256SUMS.txt` does not list itself — measured: `grep -c SHA256SUMS SHA256SUMS.txt` is 0 — so it cannot certify its own content. If it stays, the hand-back says whether that is deliberate, what it means for a reader (the file can be stale about itself and nothing would say so), and whether anything covers it.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while verifying P13-T006, which is the second time this file has been found stale by hand. THE PREMISE, measured at 72365b9 before the task was minted rather than inferred from the file's name: `grep -rln "SHA256SUMS" . --exclude-dir=target --exclude-dir=.git` returns exactly two paths, progress/HANDOFF.md and progress/state.json, and both are prose about the manifest rather than code that reads it; scripts/, .github/, crates/ and tools/ contain no reference at all; and with SHA256SUMS.txt reverted to its committed content -- which is three entries out of date, crates/sure-core/src/lib.rs line 42, docs/architecture/STORAGE_AND_DATA_PATHS.md line 72 and docs/security/PRIVACY.md line 97 -- BOTH bootstrap gates pass: `node scripts/validate-bootstrap.mjs` exits 0 with `SURE bootstrap validation OK: 17 phases, 178 tasks.` and `node scripts/taskctl.mjs validate` exits 0 with `state OK: 178 tasks`. So the file can be arbitrarily wrong and every gate this repository runs will say the tree is fine. THE MAINTENANCE TOOL IS NOT IN THE REPOSITORY, which is the sharper half: `target/tmp/regen-sums.mjs` is what builds the file, it is the only thing that does, and `target/` is gitignored -- `find . -name "regen-sums*" -not -path "./target/*"` returns nothing -- so the script exists on this machine and in no clone of this repository. The script's own header already states the gap: `SHA256SUMS.txt -- grep -r SHA256SUMS finds no script, no CI job and no test`. That sentence was written when the script was, and no task was minted for it, which is why the gap is still here. THIS LOOP HAS ALREADY SHIPPED A STALE LINE: item 74's correction on 2026-09-19 found the manifest carrying a digest for a file that had changed under it, and the fix was to regenerate rather than to give anything a reason to check. The pattern is the one this project's evidence discipline names -- a whole-tree assertion nothing can falsify reads exactly like one that is verified, and a false green is the failure mode this repository exists to catch. WHY A TASK AND NOT A ONE-LINE FIX IN THIS ACCEPTANCE: the choice is between giving the file a reader and removing it, and both have consequences that are not the supervisor's to take silently. Giving it a reader means a sixth local gate, a CI step, a committed regeneration script, and a decision about index bytes versus working-tree bytes that a wrong answer turns into permanent false reds -- and `eol=crlf` in .gitattributes makes that a real ambiguity rather than a theoretical one: scripts/install.ps1 is 2388 bytes in the index and 2426 in the checkout, so the supervisor's own first attempt at this measurement reported two mismatches that were not staleness, and the instrument was wrong rather than the file. Removing it means deleting a file that appears in MASTER_PROMPT-era bootstrap material and saying what, if anything, replaced it, which is a claim about the repository's own packaging that belongs in a task with an acceptance rather than in a verification note. Either way the honest hand-back has to measure the premise first, because the cheapest wrong answer here is to add a checker that fails on a correct tree. WINDOWS-PRIMARY AND PORTABLE, as CLAUDE.md requires: whatever the check is, it runs natively on Windows and in the ubuntu and macos CI jobs, and it does not require Git Bash, symlink privileges or administrator rights. PLACEMENT: after P15-T019, the last P15 task in array order, so the READY order stays tasks/tasks.json's order and §14 dispatches P13-T007 next. This is not a stop-the-line -- nothing here is a verdict about a user's project, and the cost of the gap is one stale line in a file that has been stale once -- so it takes the placement rule every task has taken except P15-T016.

title: Give the store a location a caller can choose
acceptance: A caller can name where SURE keeps its store, and `sure doctor` reports the location it is using. The mechanism is not project-controlled: a store that a checked project's own file could redirect is a store that a checked project could point at a place it can write.

No test in the workspace writes to the per-user store. `crates/sure-cli/tests/cli_contract.rs::hook_ingest_reads_standard_input_and_evaluates_protection` runs a real `sure hook ingest`, and that process opens and writes the developer's `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SURE\sure.db` (measured: 4096 bytes added by one isolated run, rows of kind `event` with session `cursor-session-001`). After this task the store is byte-identical across a full `cargo test --workspace`, asserted by a test rather than by a report.
The default is unchanged: a caller who names nothing gets the OS-native per-user location through the existing path abstraction, and `sure doctor` still reports it.
A location inside the project being checked is refused, as it already is on the `--goal` path, and the refusal says what did not happen.
notes: Added 2026-09-18 by the supervisor, from P7-T010's verification. Running `cargo test --workspace` on this repository writes rows into the developer's own store, and the per-user directory is read through `SHGetKnownFolderPath`, which ignores `LOCALAPPDATA`, so there is no environment variable a test can set to point a spawned SURE elsewhere. `docs/architecture/CLI.md` already described this as "the phase that gives SURE a store location a caller can choose"; no such task existed, so the gap had no owner and every gate run added to the history of the machine it ran on.

title: Carry a finding through the repair contract and the re-check
acceptance: `sure repair` on a project with an open finding answers with a repair contract, and a later `sure recheck` reports what that run left open — both observed by running the commands, not by a report about them.

The re-check list comes from the module that owns the rule (`sure_core::repair_impact`), not from a second rule written in the pipeline. `RepairContract::from_finding` refuses an empty re-check list, and that refusal is met by selecting the checks first rather than bypassed with a hand-built contract that is not actionable.

Findings are persisted, so `recheck_lifecycle::store_run` gains its caller and a second run's stage 12 compares against a real earlier run instead of an always-empty history. `recheck_lifecycle.rs`'s `store.history(&filter, 0)` call is fixed with it: `Store::history` documents 0 as "return none", so the read that is meant to find previous open findings can only ever return empty.
Stages 11 and 12 stop being `not_run` on a project that has findings, and any stage that still did not run is named in the report.
`docs/architecture/CLI.md` and `docs/architecture/CHECK_PIPELINE.md` match what the two commands do, including the status each returns.
notes: Added 2026-09-18 by the supervisor, from P7-T010's verification. P7-T010 records stage 11 as not-run and passes `rechecks: &[]` to stage 12, each with a written reason: `RepairContract::from_finding` needs the checks that can observe a finding, `repair_impact::select_impacted_checks` takes the contract it would be helping to build, and nothing writes a finding today so stage 12 has nothing to compare against. Both are honest records of a real gap rather than a false green, and the gap is what the product's repair/re-check promise (priority 8) and the queued fixture task P14-T009 are waiting on.

title: Bring the corpus's record of detector severity back in line with the detectors
acceptance: Every `detector_severity_today` value in `fixtures/adversarial/*/scenario.json` states what the named detector yields today, measured by running it — or the field is replaced by a statement of where the current value is measured. The historic fact that the required and the delivered severity were once different is not deleted: it lives in `adversarial_fixture_detection.rs`'s `SEVERITY_BEFORE_P7T011` and in git, and this task keeps it.

A test fails when a `detector_severity_today` value disagrees with the severity the detector produces, so the field cannot go stale again. It reads the fixture's own text and runs the detector; a hand-kept list of expected values in the test would be a second place to keep the same fact.

The `notes` sentences that say every detector here emits `Severity::Note`, and that `adversarial_fixture_detection.rs` "pins the gap", are corrected to what the tree now does — that test asserts the manifest's severity now, and says so.

Where a per-outcome `required_severity` cannot be met by the detector that owns the outcome, the corpus says so deliberately: `fake-auth` requires `must_fix` for `CandidateCategory::Todo` at `src/auth.js` while `demo-analytics` requires `should_fix_first` for the same category, in the same context and with the same evidence class, so no function of a proposal's own fields satisfies both. Each such outcome either restates its requirement in terms its detector can meet, or carries the reason it stands unmet and what would have to change for it to be met.

`required_severity` for the release-blocking cases is not lowered to match today's implementation, and `evaluation/acceptance-manifest.json` is unchanged by this task. A corpus edited to agree with the code is the false green this repository exists to catch, one level up.
notes: Added 2026-09-18 by the supervisor, from P7-T011's verification. P7-T011 gave detector findings the severity the corpus required, and in doing so made the corpus's own record of what the detectors do false: `fixtures/adversarial/{fake-payment,fake-auth,fake-email,dead-button,route-mismatch,demo-analytics}/scenario.json` still carry `detector_severity_today: "note"`, and their `notes` sentences still say every detector emits `Severity::Note` and that `adversarial_fixture_detection.rs` pins the gap between that and the requirement. No `.rs` file reads the field, so nothing depended on it — which is exactly why it could go stale unnoticed. The same verification measured the finer statement that remains unmet: in those fixtures the `candidate_scanner` outcomes land at `can_fix_later` while their per-outcome `required_severity` says `must_fix`, and the release-blocking severity arrives through the detector that saw the substituted action itself. `finding_gravity`'s module doc records why the `Todo` case cannot be satisfied by both fixtures at once. P7-T011 deliberately did not edit any of this: the fixtures were off-limits to its worker because a task that measures against a requirement should not be the task that rewrites it afterwards.

title: Let the check report read the capability tier from the project's recorded events
acceptance: `sure check` on a project whose store holds a session's harness events reports the tier those events earn, and with no events it still reports the snapshot tier — both observed by running the command against a project with recorded events and one without, not by a report about them.

The tier comes from `capability_report::report_from_events`, which computes it from the events SURE actually received and refuses a self-reported `Protected` tier; the pipeline does not grow a second rule, and the adapter's own claim is never taken upward.
The blind spots that module already computes are reported beside the tier, so a tier says what it does not cover rather than reading as completeness.
The capability line names what it counted — which harnesses the events came from and over what window — so a reader can tell 'no events were recorded' from 'events exist and were not counted'.

Every document that states a tier claim for a harness (`integrations/*/README.md`, `docs/architecture/MCP_BRIDGE.md`, `docs/architecture/CLI.md`) matches what the report now says, including the case where the events exist but the tier did not rise.
notes: Added 2026-09-18 by the supervisor, from P12-T007's verification. The Codex bridge now reaches Tier 1 on ingest — four events normalised, stored and readable — while `sure check` still prints "capability tier 0, snapshot" for a project that has them, because the pipeline takes the tier from the command line and `crates/sure-core/src/capability_report.rs::report_from_events` has no callers. The same holds for the Claude Code and Cursor bridges (P10-T003, P11-T004), whose accepted work mapped events to a tier the report does not read. This is the safe direction — understating what SURE knows — but it means each integration's tier table promises something the verdict does not deliver, and a reader who records a session and then checks the project is told nothing changed. Related, and separate: `agent.claim` and `user.request` have no production caller, which is why Codex's `Stop` and prompt submissions are refused rather than mapped; giving claims a consumer is its own task and is not required for this one.
